claim: The right-to-left column-operation induction plan proves the full Vandermonde determinant identity for every positive integer n and all real x_1,...,x_n.
evidence: Induct on n. For n=1 the determinant is 1 and the product is empty, hence 1. For n>=2, in the displayed Vandermonde matrix perform C_k <- C_k-x_1 C_{k-1} for k=n,n-1,...,2. Descending order ensures C_{k-1} is an unchanged original column when used, and each operation preserves the determinant. The first row becomes (1,0,...,0). For row i>=2, the new entry in column k>=2 is x_i^{k-1}-x_1 x_i^{k-2}=(x_i-x_1)x_i^{k-2}. Expanding along the first row and factoring x_i-x_1 from each remaining row gives det = (product over i=2,...,n of (x_i-x_1)) times the Vandermonde determinant on x_2,...,x_n. The induction hypothesis changes the latter to the product over 2<=i<j<=n of (x_j-x_i). Multiplying gives exactly the product over 1<=i<j<=n.

author: high2
claim: The Vandermonde determinant identity follows by induction after descending column operations expose all factors involving x_1.
evidence:
Plan ID: direct-induction. Status: solved.

Subgoal 1 (base case): For n=1, the determinant is det(1)=1 and the product over the empty set is 1.

Subgoal 2 (induction step): Assume the identity for n-1 arbitrary real inputs and let D_n denote the determinant in the claim. Number its columns C_1,...,C_n. In descending order k=n,n-1,...,2, replace C_k by C_k-x_1C_{k-1}. Each replacement preserves the determinant: by linearity in C_k, the change subtracts x_1 times a determinant having two equal columns, hence subtracts zero. The descending order ensures that, when the operation for k is made, both columns involved still have their original power entries. Thus the transformed entry in row i and column k>=2 is x_i^{k-1}-x_1x_i^{k-2}=(x_i-x_1)x_i^{k-2}. Its first row is (1,0,...,0). Expanding along that row gives a minor whose row indexed by i in {2,...,n} is (x_i-x_1)(1,x_i,...,x_i^{n-2}). Factoring x_i-x_1 from every such row and applying the induction hypothesis to x_2,...,x_n yields
D_n = [product_{i=2}^n (x_i-x_1)] [product_{2<=i<j<=n}(x_j-x_i)] = product_{1<=i<j<=n}(x_j-x_i).

No counterexample search was needed because every subgoal was solved directly. No external theorem was used.

author: high4
claim: Solved direct-induction proof attempt for the complete Vandermonde determinant identity.
evidence:
Plan ID: direct-induction.
Attempt type: direct.
Subgoal: prove the full Vandermonde determinant identity for every positive integer n and all real x_1,...,x_n.
Status: solved.
Attempt summary and proof: Use induction on n. For n=1, the determinant is 1 and the product over no pairs is 1. Let n>=2 and assume the identity for n-1 real numbers. In the displayed n by n matrix, subtract the first row from every row indexed i=2,...,n. Expanding the resulting determinant along the first column gives the determinant of the (n-1) by (n-1) matrix whose row indexed by i (i=2,...,n) is
(x_i-x_1, x_i^2-x_1^2, ..., x_i^{n-1}-x_1^{n-1}).
For every integer k with 1<=k<=n-1,
x_i^k-x_1^k=(x_i-x_1)(x_i^{k-1}+x_i^{k-2}x_1+...+x_1^{k-1}).
By multilinearity, factor x_i-x_1 from each row. The remaining matrix has k-th column equal, at row i, to
x_i^{k-1}+x_i^{k-2}x_1+...+x_1^{k-1}.
Starting with k=n-1 and proceeding downward to k=2, replace column k by column k minus x_1 times column k-1. Descending order ensures column k-1 has not yet changed, so its new entry is exactly x_i^{k-1}; column 1 is already 1. These column operations preserve the determinant and transform the remaining matrix into the Vandermonde matrix on x_2,...,x_n. The induction hypothesis therefore makes its determinant
product_{2<=i<j<=n}(x_j-x_i).
Multiplying the extracted row factors yields
product_{j=2}^n(x_j-x_1) product_{2<=i<j<=n}(x_j-x_i)
=product_{1<=i<j<=n}(x_j-x_i),
which is the required identity. No division or distinctness assumption is used.

author: high7
claim: Solved direct proof of the full Vandermonde determinant identity by induction using descending column operations.
evidence:
We prove the identity by induction on the positive integer \(n\).

For \(n=1\), the determinant is \(\det(1)=1\). The product on the right is over the empty set of pairs and therefore equals \(1\).

Now let \(n\ge 2\), and assume the stated identity holds for \(n-1\) and every choice of \(n-1\) real numbers. In the displayed \(n\times n\) determinant, successively for \(j=n,n-1,\ldots,2\), replace column \(j\) by column \(j\) minus \(x_1\) times column \(j-1\). These operations are performed in descending order, so at the operation indexed by \(j\), both column \(j\) and column \(j-1\) still have their original entries \(x_i^{j-1}\) and \(x_i^{j-2}\), respectively. Adding a scalar multiple of one column to another does not change a determinant. Hence the determinant is unchanged, while its entry in row \(i\) and column \(j\ge 2\) becomes
\[
x_i^{j-1}-x_1x_i^{j-2}=(x_i-x_1)x_i^{j-2}.
\]
For \(i=1\), this entry is \(0\), so the first row after the operations is \((1,0,\ldots,0)\).

Expanding along that first row (whose nonzero entry is in position \((1,1)\) and has cofactor sign \(+1\)) gives
\[
\det\!\begin{pmatrix}
1 & x_1 & \cdots & x_1^{n-1}\\
\vdots & \vdots & & \vdots\\
1 & x_n & \cdots & x_n^{n-1}
\end{pmatrix}
=
\det\!\bigl((x_i-x_1)x_i^{j-2}\bigr)_{\substack{2\le i\le n\\2\le j\le n}}.
\]
Factoring \(x_i-x_1\) from the row indexed by each \(i=2,\ldots,n\) yields
\[
\left(\prod_{i=2}^{n}(x_i-x_1)\right)
\det\!\begin{pmatrix}
1 & x_2 & x_2^2 & \cdots & x_2^{n-2}\\
1 & x_3 & x_3^2 & \cdots & x_3^{n-2}\\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
1 & x_n & x_n^2 & \cdots & x_n^{n-2}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The induction hypothesis, applied to the \(n-1\) real numbers \(x_2,\ldots,x_n\), identifies the remaining determinant as
\[
\prod_{2\le i<j\le n}(x_j-x_i).
\]
Therefore the original determinant equals
\[
\left(\prod_{i=2}^{n}(x_i-x_1)\right)
\left(\prod_{2\le i<j\le n}(x_j-x_i)\right)
=
\prod_{1\le i<j\le n}(x_j-x_i),
\]
because the first product contains exactly the factors indexed by pairs with first index \(1\), and the second contains exactly the factors indexed by pairs with first index at least \(2\). This completes the induction. No division was used, so the argument also covers choices in which some of the real numbers are equal.

author: high
claim: The complete Vandermonde determinant identity is solved by induction using the determinant as a polynomial in the final-row parameter.
evidence:
Use induction on \(n\). For \(n=1\), the determinant is \(1\), equal to the empty product. Assume the identity for size \(n-1\). If two of \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) are equal, the determinant has two equal rows and is \(0\), while the product contains a zero factor, so the identity holds. Now suppose the \(x_i\) are pairwise distinct. Define
\[
p(t)=\det\!\begin{pmatrix}
1&x_1&\cdots&x_1^{n-1}\\
\vdots&\vdots&&\vdots\\
1&x_{n-1}&\cdots&x_{n-1}^{n-1}\\
1&t&\cdots&t^{n-1}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
It is a polynomial in \(t\) of degree at most \(n-1\). For each \(i<n\), substituting \(t=x_i\) gives two equal rows, hence \(p(x_i)=0\). Since these \(n-1\) roots are distinct, \(p(t)=c\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}(t-x_i)\) for some coefficient \(c\). The coefficient of \(t^{n-1}\) in \(p\) is the cofactor of the last-row, last-column entry. Its sign is \((-1)^{n+n}=1\), and its minor is the size-\(n-1\) Vandermonde determinant. By induction,
\[
c=\prod_{1\le i<j\le n-1}(x_j-x_i).
\]
Putting \(t=x_n\) gives
\[
p(x_n)=\prod_{1\le i<j\le n-1}(x_j-x_i)\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}(x_n-x_i)
=\prod_{1\le i<j\le n}(x_j-x_i).
\]
This is the required determinant.

links.attempt_summary: Separate the repeated-input case; in the distinct case factor the final-row determinant polynomial by its n-1 roots and identify its leading coefficient by cofactor expansion.

glossary.c: the leading coefficient of p(t), identified with the size-(n-1) Vandermonde determinant

For n>=2, write the matrix columns as C_1,...,C_n and, in the order j=n,n-1,...,2, replace C_j by C_j-x_1 C_{j-1}. Since only columns of index greater than j have already changed, C_{j-1} is the original column when used. The determinant is unchanged. The first row becomes (1,0,...,0). For i>=2 and j>=2 the new (i,j)-entry is (x_i-x_1)x_i^(j-2). Cofactor expansion at the first row and extraction of one factor from each remaining row give det_n=(product_{i=2}^n(x_i-x_1))det_{n-1}(x_2,...,x_n). The induction hypothesis turns the latter determinant into product_{2<=i<j<=n}(x_j-x_i). Multiplying gives product_{1<=i<j<=n}(x_j-x_i).
